analysis.one_liner: Requires federally funded drug research to come with agreements keeping US prices at reasonable levels.
analysis.headline: The bill would cap US prices of drugs developed with federal research funding at the median price charged in Canada and six other large, wealthy countries; it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on August 13, 2026, and has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires any company or institution that develops a drug, vaccine, or medical device using federal research money to sign a "reasonable pricing" agreement with the Secretary of Health and Human Services. The agreement must keep the US price at or below the median price charged in Canada and six other big, high-income OECD countries. It also forces companies that commercialize taxpayer-funded inventions to report their clinical trial costs, federal subsidies, and annual sales revenues, and to make those reports public.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need drugs, vaccines, gene therapies, and devices that were invented with federal research dollars, since US prices could no longer exceed prices in peer countries. Taxpayers also gain because Medicare, Medicaid, and private premiums pay less for products built on research they funded. The transparency reports would give the public, for the first time, a clear picture of what taxpayer-funded inventions cost to develop and earn.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers who fund medical research

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal research grant, contract, or patent license for a biomedical product to include a reasonable pricing obligation, with the Secretary of Health and Human Services deciding what counts as reasonable.

Caps the US price of a federally funded product at the median price charged in Canada and six other large, high-income OECD countries, so Americans can no longer pay the highest price in the developed world for a drug they helped invent.
Allows the Secretary to add rules that lower prices when revenues exceed targets, when price exceeds a cost-per-health-benefit standard, or when prices are a barrier to access.
Requires manufacturers of taxpayer-funded products to report clinical trial costs, federal subsidies, and annual revenues by country, and requires the government to make those reports public.
Applies broadly to drugs, vaccines, medical devices, diagnostic tests, cell- and gene-based therapies, and other health technologies developed with federal support.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies and universities that license federally funded inventions would earn less from products whose prices had exceeded international levels. Some revenue that currently flows from higher US prices to patent-holders and their licensees would instead stay with patients, insurers, and government health programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug companies and university patent-licensing offices

drawbacks.text: The bill itself acknowledges the tension: the Secretary must balance lower prices against 'robust incentives to invest in biomedical research and development.' If pricing agreements cut into expected returns, companies may license fewer federally funded inventions or shift work to channels outside federal funding.

The bill concedes an administration problem: in cases where third parties control the relevant intellectual property or know-how, enforcing a pricing agreement is difficult, and the Secretary is told to take those 'challenges of administering' into account — meaning some products could escape the price cap in practice.

The Secretary can waive the pricing obligation for any product after notice, comment, and an economic analysis showing the waiver is in the public interest. That discretion means a sympathetic administration could grant waivers broadly, while the pricing formula's reference-price mechanism could also be modified by regulation.
The bill only covers products developed with federal research funding, so it would not touch the many drugs developed entirely with private money, leaving most drug prices unchanged.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: Americans would stop paying world-leading prices for the subset of medical products invented with their own tax dollars, and would finally see the cost and revenue data behind those products. The cost is a modestly weaker financial return on federally funded inventions, which industry argues could reduce commercialization — a trade-off Congress confronted in the 1990s when the NIH dropped a similar reasonable-pricing clause. The waiver process and the third-party intellectual-property problem give an administration room to soften the policy, so how much patients actually save depends heavily on how the Secretary of the day enforces it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not held a hearing, marked it up, or scheduled a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle of Oregon introduced the bill on August 13, 2026, joined as original cosponsors by Democratic Reps. Doggett, Stansbury, Takano, Norton, Tlaib, Jayapal, and Casar.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over prescription drug policy.
Fourteen House Democrats in total have signed on as cosponsors; no Republican has.
The committee has taken no further action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed for anyone. The companies and universities that charge current prices for federally funded inventions are better off only in the sense that no pricing requirement has been enacted; patients and taxpayers remain in the same position as before the bill was filed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet; current drug pricing stands

for.name: Rep. Val Hoyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its central mechanism: pricing agreements on federally funded biomedical research.

for.name: Reps. Doggett, Stansbury, Takano, Norton, Tlaib, Jayapal, and Casar
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 13, 2026, and has taken no action since — no hearing, markup, or vote is on the record.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research industry
against.what_they_did: No lobbying on this specific bill appears in the provided record, but the pharmaceutical industry has long opposed reasonable-pricing conditions on federally funded research; the NIH adopted and then abandoned such a clause in the 1990s amid industry objections.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 14 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, but no vote has occurred, so the partisan split has not yet been tested.

industries.note: Companies would no longer be able to charge US patients prices above the median charged in Canada and six peer countries for products invented with federal research money. Today Americans often pay the highest prices in the world for exactly those products, so the cap transfers revenue from patent-holders to patients and government health programs.

industries.industry: University technology-transfer and research licensing offices
industries.note: Universities earn licensing royalties on inventions made with federal grants, and the bill attaches pricing conditions to those licenses. Some licensing revenue would shrink, though the same research institutions depend on federal funding that the bill does not cut.
Lower prices on federally invented drugs would reduce what insurers, employer plans, Medicare, and Medicaid pay, easing premiums and program spending.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with 14 cosponsors, all Democrats, in a chamber where Republicans hold a majority. A drug-pricing bill of this kind typically needs a committee hearing and markup before it can reach the floor, and none has been scheduled; absent a major push, the likely path is that it stays in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027, though a companion Senate bill or inclusion in a larger package could keep the idea alive.
